items.english: "No, ever since I was a child . . ." As Liu was about to say something, the barbarian monk cut him off.
"Drink as you may, you never get drunk, do you?"
" . . ." Liu stared hard at the other's face and shut his mouth. In fact, drink as he might, this man had never been drunk.

"That is the proof of the disease," the barbarian monk went on with a faint smile. "There is a wine worm in your belly. Unless it is removed, this disease will not be cured. This poor monk has come to cure your disease."
notes: Kept the monk's humble clerical self-reference as "This poor monk" for 貧道 rather than flattening to "I".

items.english: "Can it be cured?" Liu let out the words in an uncertain voice before he knew it. And he was ashamed of himself for it.
"It is because it can be cured that I have come."
Then Sun Sensei, who until now had listened in silence to the exchange, suddenly put in a word.
"No, there will be no need to use anything like medicine," the barbarian monk answered curtly.

Sun Sensei, to begin with, despised the two teachings of Dao and Buddha with scarcely any reason. So even when thrown together with a Daoist priest or a monk, he had very rarely exchanged a word. That he should now suddenly feel moved to speak was wholly because the words "wine worm" had caught his interest; fond of wine himself, on hearing this he had grown a little uneasy lest there be a wine worm in his own belly too. When he heard the barbarian monk's grudging answer, however, he suddenly felt as if he had been made a fool of, so with a slight frown he began once more, in silence as before, to place his stones. And at the same time, inwardly, he thought his host Liu a fool for meeting with so insolent a monk.
